This is an official CDC health advisory. The Centers for Disease Control and Prevention (CDC) is issuing this Health Alert Network (HAN) Health Advisory to notify clinicians, public health officials, and potential travelers about a measles outbreak in Texas and New Mexico and offer guidance for prevention and monitoring. As of March 7, 2025, Texas and New Mexico have reported 208 confirmed cases associated with this outbreak (198 in Texas and 10 in New Mexico). top_result_summaries.snippet: The first measles outbreaks of the new year were reported this month, according to data from the Centers for Disease Control and Prevention, which identified a rise in cases of the highly contagious disease that has cropped up in 17 states. Measles cases have been confirmed in 17 states this year. Cases reached as high as 254 during the week of Jan. 11, according to the CDC, a stark difference between the highest number of cases recorded in a single week last year, when 115 cases were confirmed the week of March 30. Two new outbreaks, which the CDC defines as three or more related cases, recorded this year have resulted in eight confirmed measles cases, as the vast majority of confirmed cases are associated with outbreaks that began in 2025. Unvaccinated people with the confirmed measles cases account for 94% of this year’s cases so far. South Carolina has the majority of measles cases in the U.S. so far this year, with 467 confirmed by the CDC.

top_result_summaries.title: CDC social media silence during 2025 measles outbreak left void filled by news media, study suggests | CIDRAP
top_result_summaries.snippet: # CDC social media silence during 2025 measles outbreak left void filled by news media, study suggests. As the United States faces its largest measles outbreak in three decades, one of the nation’s most storied public health voices has largely fallen silent on social media. A new exploratory analysis suggests that the Centers for Disease Control and Prevention (CDC) dramatically scaled back its social media posts during the first seven months of 2025, creating what researchers call a “health communication void.” That empty space was quickly filled by news media and, in some cases, less-credible voices. The study, published in *Vaccine*, examined measles and measles, mumps, and rubella (MMR) vaccine-related posts from official CDC accounts on Facebook, Instagram, and X, alongside posts from major news outlets. What’s more, none of the CDC’s 2025 social media posts supported MMR vaccination, the most effective way to prevent measles infection.

top_result_summaries.title: 2025 Southwest United States measles outbreak - Wikipedia
top_result_summaries.snippet: # 2025 Southwest United States measles outbreak. | 2025–26 United States measles outbreak | |. | Location | United States (Texas, New Mexico, Oklahoma, Kansas), Mexico (Chihuahua "Chihuahua (state)")) |. In January 2025, cases of measles began to appear in Texas and neighboring states in the United States. The outbreak became one of the largest in the country since 2000, when the United States declared the disease eliminated in the country. In March, cases linked to the outbreak were announced in Oklahoma, the Mexican state of Chihuahua "Chihuahua (state)"), and Kansas. Cases were concentrated in the Texas Mennonite community, and officials believed the disease was first imported from an outbreak in a Mennonite community in Ontario, Canada. More than 99 individuals were hospitalized, and three died: two children in Lubbock (a six-year-old and an eight-year-old) and an adult in Lea County, New Mexico. The Texas outbreak involved the measles genotype D8, and was linked to cases in New Mexico, Kansas, Oklahoma, and Chihuahua, Mexico "Chihuahua (state)").

top_result_summaries.title: Measles - United States of America
top_result_summaries.snippet: On 11 March 2025, the World Health Organization (WHO) received a report from the International Health Regulation (2005) (IHR) National Focal Point (NFP) of the United States of America (United States) on the ongoing measles outbreak in the country, notified under IHR because it is an unusual event with potential significant public health impact, with the number of cases and deaths in 2025 exceeding the numbers in previous years. Additionally, cases linked to the outbreak in the State of Texas, United States, have been reported in Mexico. From 1 January to 20 March 2025, 17 States have reported a total of 378 cases of measles, including two deaths - the first deaths related to measles in the United States in a decade. The majority of cases are in children who are unvaccinated or have unknown vaccination status, and the overall hospitalization rate is 17%. On 11 March 2025, the NFP of the United States notified to WHO an ongoing outbreak of measles in the United States.

A second iteration targeting these specific gaps is warranted within the remaining query budget (max 4 queries, iteration 2 of 2).
decision.coverage_assessment: Good national-level coverage: CDC HAN (March 7, 208 cases TX+NM), CDC MMWR (April 17, 800 cases, 3 deaths, 85 hospitalizations), WHO DON (March 20, 378 cases, 2 deaths, 17% hospitalization rate), Wikipedia (outbreak narrative, 3 deaths, 99+ hospitalizations), JHU IVAC tracker (county-level data since Jan 1 2025). Gaps: (a) PAHO epidemiological alert text not confirmed; (b) Oklahoma, New Mexico state health department pages absent; (c) Texas DSHS page appeared but no confirming snippet for Q1 date-stamped case counts; (d) Early Q1 (January–February) subnational snapshots missing; (e) ProMED/HealthMap entries not surfaced; (f) Death corroboration from state sources (Texas DSHS, NM DOH) not confirmed.
decision.source_diversity_assessment: Source types present: official CDC (3 domains), WHO (2), Wikipedia (2), JHU academic tracker (3), CIDRAP (3), PAHO (3 hits but no confirming snippet), state health (2: TX, SC), news (Forbes, abc7, contagionlive), PMC literature (3), AAP (1). decision.trustworthiness_assessment: High-trust sources confirmed: cdc.gov (HAN advisory, MMWR, data page), who.int (DON), publichealth.jhu.edu (IVAC tracker citing official sources). Medium-trust: Wikipedia (well-cited for this outbreak), CIDRAP (reputable academic news). Lower-trust for case counts: Forbes, contagionlive, YouTube (useful for context only). PAHO hits not yet confirmed as containing Q1-specific data. State .gov pages (dshs.texas.gov, dph.sc.gov) appeared but snippets not confirmed.
decision.disease_location_time_fit_assessment: Disease fit: excellent (all results are measles-specific). Location fit: good (US national and TX/NM/OK subnational). Time fit: mostly good — CDC HAN (Mar 7) and WHO DON (Mar 20) fall squarely in Q1; MMWR (Apr 17) extends slightly beyond but covers Q1 data. Some results (Forbes, contagionlive) reference 2025 totals beyond Q1 and must be used carefully. Early Q1 (Jan–Feb) subnational snapshots are underrepresented.
decision.corroboration_potential_assessment: The WHO DON snippet (378 cases, 2 deaths, Jan 1–Mar 20) and CDC HAN snippet (208 cases, Mar 7) are mutually consistent and corroborate each other for the Q1 window. The MMWR figure (800 cases by Apr 17) extends beyond Q1 but provides hospitalization (85) and death (3) totals that partially overlap Q1. Wikipedia's 3-death figure (2 Lubbock children + 1 Lea County adult) aligns with MMWR. State-level corroboration for Texas and New Mexico deaths is still needed from official state sources. PAHO and ProMED would add independent cross-validation.

top_result_summaries.title: 2025 Southwest United States measles outbreak - Wikipedia
top_result_summaries.snippet: # 2025 Southwest United States measles outbreak. | 2025–26 United States measles outbreak | |. | Location | United States (Texas, New Mexico, Oklahoma, Kansas), Mexico (Chihuahua "Chihuahua (state)")) |. In January 2025, cases of measles began to appear in Texas and neighboring states in the United States. The outbreak became one of the largest in the country since 2000, when the United States declared the disease eliminated in the country. In March, cases linked to the outbreak were announced in Oklahoma, the Mexican state of Chihuahua "Chihuahua (state)"), and Kansas. Cases were concentrated in the Texas Mennonite community, and officials believed the disease was first imported from an outbreak in a Mennonite community in Ontario, Canada. More than 99 individuals were hospitalized, and three died: two children in Lubbock (a six-year-old and an eight-year-old) and an adult in Lea County, New Mexico. The Texas outbreak involved the measles genotype D8, and was linked to cases in New Mexico, Kansas, Oklahoma, and Chihuahua, Mexico "Chihuahua (state)").

top_result_summaries.title: Measles Outbreak in a Child Care Facility — Lubbock, Texas, March–April 2025  | MMWR
top_result_summaries.snippet: During March–April 2025, eight confirmed measles cases linked to a child care facility were reported in Lubbock, Texas. On March 21, 2025, Lubbock Public Health (LPH) in Texas received a report of a child care attendee aged 3 years, with fever, rash, cough, coryza, conjunctivitis, otitis media, and diarrhea who received a positive test result for measles by real-time reverse transcription–polymerase chain reaction (RT-PCR). Six additional children who attended the same child care facility and the grandfather of one of the children were confirmed by RT-PCR testing to have measles. On March 21, 2025, Lubbock Public Health (LPH) in Texas was notified of a suspected measles case in a child aged 3 years (index patient, patient A) who had fever, rash, cough, coryza, conjunctivitis, otitis media, and diarrhea. During March 25–29, LPH was notified of two additional suspected measles cases (patients B and C); both cases occurred in children who attended the same child care facility as the index patient, including a child in the same classroom as the index patient (patient B) and a sibling of the index patient (patient C) who was exposed at home (Table).

decision.decision_reason: Two full iterations have been executed (8 queries total), reaching the max_iterations bound of 2. More importantly, the accumulated evidence across both iterations is substantively sufficient to populate all target fields for the Q1 2025 (2025-01-01 to 2025-03-31) window. Key authoritative sources have been surfaced across all required source-type categories: (1) CDC official surveillance — HAN advisory (208 confirmed cases as of March 7, Texas + New Mexico), CDC measles data page, and two MMWR reports (West Texas Jan 20–Mar 18: 325 cases, 60 hospitalizations, 1 death; Lubbock child care facility March 2025: 8 cases); (2) WHO Disease Outbreak News DON561 (378 cases, 2 deaths, 17 states, Jan 1–Mar 20, 2025); (3) Texas DSHS outbreak page (Feb 26 death press release confirmed, April 6 second death press release noted — first death in late February falls within Q1); (4) New Mexico DOH (nmhealth.org) — first NM case confirmed Lea County February 11, 2025; (5) PAHO appeared 6 times in iteration 2 (highest domain frequency), providing international-org validation; (6) Multiple MMWR peer-reviewed reports with precise date ranges, case counts, hospitalization rates, and death details within Q1; (7) News corroboration from ABC7NY and ABCNews for the first Texas death (late February, within Q1) and second death (April, outside Q1). The JHU IVAC US Measles Tracker (publichealth.jhu.edu) provides a structured county-level aggregation from official sources since January 1, 2025. All primary target fields — disease, country, subnational_location, locality, date_reported, cases_confirmed, deaths, hospitalizations, source_url, source_type, evidence_quote — have sufficient evidence anchors. Remaining minor gaps (Oklahoma state DOH page, PAHO snippet text, ProMED archive entries) are unlikely to materially change the Q1 evidence picture given the strong CDC/WHO/MMWR/state-DOH coverage already achieved, and the iteration budget is exhausted.
decision.coverage_assessment: Strong. All major target fields are covered by at least one authoritative source: (a) cases_confirmed — CDC HAN (208 as of Mar 7), MMWR West Texas (325 Jan 20–Mar 18), WHO DON (378 Jan 1–Mar 20), DSHS Texas page; (b) deaths — WHO DON (2 deaths through Mar 20, within Q1), ABC7NY/ABCNews (first Texas child death late February = within Q1; second Texas death April = outside Q1), MMWR West Texas (1 death within Jan–Mar window); (c) hospitalizations — MMWR West Texas (60/325 = 18.5%), WHO DON (17% overall rate), CDC HAN (18 hospitalized at 124-case snapshot); (d) subnational_location — Texas (West Texas / South Plains / Lubbock), New Mexico (Lea County), Oklahoma, Kansas mentioned; (e) date_reported — multiple date-stamped snapshots across January–March 2025; (f) source_url — cdc.gov (HAN, MMWR ×2, data page), who.int (DON561), dshs.texas.gov, nmhealth.org (×2), publichealth.jhu.edu, abc7ny.com, abcnews.com, cidrap.umn.edu; (g) source_type — official_public_health_agency, international_organization_report, peer_reviewed_literature (MMWR), news_and_situation_report, structured_tracker all represented.
decision.source_diversity_assessment: Good diversity across source types: official federal agency (CDC), official state agencies (Texas DSHS, NM DOH), international organization (WHO, PAHO candidate), peer-reviewed surveillance literature (MMWR ×2), structured tracker (JHU IVAC), and news (ABC7NY, ABCNews, CIDRAP). Geographic diversity covers national aggregate (CDC, WHO) and subnational (Texas West Plains/Lubbock, New Mexico Lea County). The JHU IVAC tracker adds county-level granularity from aggregated official sources. Oklahoma and Kansas state DOH pages were not surfaced, but those states' cases are captured in the national aggregates (CDC HAN, WHO DON).
decision.trustworthiness_assessment: High. Primary evidence anchors are CDC (cdc.gov — HAN advisory, MMWR ×2, data page), WHO (who.int — DON561), Texas DSHS (dshs.texas.gov), and New Mexico DOH (nmhealth.org). These are the highest-authority sources for US measles surveillance. MMWR reports are peer-reviewed CDC publications with precise date ranges and case counts. News sources (ABC7NY, ABCNews) cite DSHS press releases directly and are used only for corroboration of death timing. JHU IVAC tracker compiles from official state/county sources. PAHO appeared 6 times but no confirming snippet text was returned — treat as a candidate source pending content verification rather than a confirmed evidence anchor. Reddit and respiratory-therapy.com are lower-trust and should be used only as corroborating signals, not primary evidence.
decision.disease_location_time_fit_assessment: Excellent fit. All surfaced sources explicitly reference measles in the United States during 2025, with multiple sources providing date-stamped snapshots within the strict Q1 window (Jan 1–Mar 31, 2025): WHO DON covers Jan 1–Mar 20; MMWR West Texas covers Jan 20–Mar 18; CDC HAN snapshot is Mar 7; NM DOH first case is Feb 11; DSHS first death press release is Feb 26; Lubbock child care MMWR begins Mar 21 (straddles Q1 end). The MMWR Jan–Apr 17 report extends beyond Q1 but its Q1-attributable subset is bounded by the WHO DON figure (378 cases through Mar 20) as a reliable lower bound. The Forbes article (dated 2026-01-30) and contagionlive.com article reference 2025 as a prior year and are not Q1-primary sources.
decision.corroboration_potential_assessment: The core Q1 2025 figures are well-corroborated across independent sources: (1) The 378-case / 2-death figure (Jan 1–Mar 20) from WHO DON is consistent with the CDC HAN 208-case snapshot (Mar 7) as a lower bound and the MMWR 325-case West Texas figure (Jan 20–Mar 18) as a partial subset. (2) The first Texas child death in late February is corroborated by the DSHS Feb 26 press release reference (dshs.texas.gov snippet), ABC7NY article, and ABCNews article — all citing DSHS. (3) The NM Lea County first case (Feb 11) is confirmed by nmhealth.org directly. (4) The MMWR West Texas report independently confirms 325 cases and 60 hospitalizations within the strict Q1 window (Jan 20–Mar 18). Minor discrepancy: WHO DON reports 2 deaths through Mar 20; MMWR Jan–Apr 17 reports 3 deaths total; the third death (NM adult, Lea County) timing relative to Mar 31 is uncertain from snippets alone — state-level NM DOH page (nmhealth.org) is a candidate source to resolve this but snippet did not confirm death date.
decision.stop_reason: Max iterations (2) reached and evidence coverage is substantively sufficient across all target fields and required source-type categories for the Q1 2025 window.
